## 4. Quality Plan

### 4.1 Testing Strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the framework-independent domain core and application policies. They will test:

- maximum three hours per day per user;
- overlapping reservation detection;
- reservation ownership and modification rules;
- opening-hour restrictions;
- recurring block-booking expansion;
- 48-hour staff override rules;
- cancellation and modification state transitions;
- equipment and capacity matching;
- idempotency of commands;
- handling of time zones and daylight-saving transitions.

Repositories, clocks, identity providers and notification services will be represented by in-memory fakes or mocks. These tests directly satisfy QR-5 because no database or network is required.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Integration tests will verify real adapter behaviour against disposable services or test instances:

- PostgreSQL schema, indexes, transactions and conflict constraints;
- SAML assertion parsing and role mapping using representative test assertions;
- iCal parsing, recurring events and malformed-feed handling;
- legacy inventory read-only access;
- email and push-provider request formatting;
- kiosk polling and SSE behaviour;
- outbox retry and deduplication.

Database tests will specifically run concurrent reservation attempts for the same room and time window to ensure only one succeeds.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will be defined for:

- the public HTTP API, including status codes such as `409 Conflict`;
- the kiosk schedule response and update protocol;
- SAML claim expectations;
- iCal feed assumptions;
- notification-provider interfaces.

Consumer-style tests will ensure that changes to an adapter or endpoint do not silently break its consumers. The contract tests are particularly important because CLRS depends on systems outside the team’s control.

#### End-to-end tests

A small set of end-to-end tests will run against a deployed test environment. Scenarios will include:

1. authenticate through the test SAML identity provider;
2. search for a room;
3. reserve it;
4. verify that a second overlapping reservation receives a conflict;
5. modify and cancel the reservation;
6. create a staff block booking and verify affected reservations follow the approved policy;
7. confirm a kiosk receives the changed schedule;
8. confirm a reminder is scheduled;
9. export a utilisation report.

End-to-end tests will focus on critical journeys rather than duplicating every unit-test case.

#### Performance, resilience and security tests

A load test will simulate at least 2,000 concurrent users at semester-start traffic levels, measuring availability-search p95 and error rate. The acceptance target is p95 below 400 ms under the defined workload.

Resilience tests will disable the iCal feed, notification provider and kiosk network to verify that reservations remain usable and kiosks display cached data. Security tests will include unauthorised staff endpoints, SAML replay or invalid assertion cases, injection attempts and checks that PII does not appear in logs.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use short-lived feature branches merged into a protected `main` branch through pull requests. Each pull request requires review by the other team member, a successful CI pipeline and an updated design or API note when behaviour changes.

CI gates will include:

- compilation and static analysis;
- unit tests;
- adapter and database integration tests;
- API contract tests;
- security dependency scanning;
- migration validation;
- a smoke deployment to a temporary environment.

The pipeline will publish an immutable container image only after all required gates pass. Database migrations must be backward-compatible with the previous application version. Destructive changes will be separated into later migrations.

Production deployment will use a rolling or blue-green strategy:

1. build and tag an immutable release;
2. deploy to a staging environment;
3. run smoke and health checks;
4. deploy to a second production instance or inactive environment;
5. check readiness, database connectivity and key metrics;
6. shift traffic gradually;
7. monitor errors, latency and reservation conflict rates.

Rollback means redirecting traffic to the previous image and disabling the new release. The previous image and migration status will be retained. A rollback rehearsal will be performed before release and must complete within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Structured logs will include timestamp, severity, service version, correlation ID, endpoint, duration, response status and opaque entity identifiers. Logs will record operational failures such as database errors, failed imports, outbox retries and notification failures.

Logs will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation descriptions or other PII. Staff audit records will be stored separately with controlled access and a documented retention period.

#### Metrics

The system will measure:

- request count, error rate and latency by endpoint;
- availability during configured opening hours;
- search p50, p95 and p99 latency;
- number of concurrent requests;
- database query duration and connection-pool saturation;
- reservation conflict rate;
- outbox backlog and oldest unprocessed event age;
- kiosk update age by room;
- number of kiosks using cached schedules;
- iCal and inventory import success, duration and freshness;
- reminder success and failure rates;
- CPU, memory and database storage utilisation.

#### Alerts

Alerts will include:

- monthly availability forecast below 99.5%;
- elevated five-minute error rate;
- availability-search p95 above 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under normal traffic;
- database connection pool above 80% for five minutes;
- outbox oldest item older than 30 seconds;
- any kiosk schedule update older than 10 seconds while the kiosk is connected;
- inventory or calendar data older than an agreed freshness threshold;
- repeated SAML authentication failures;
- logs detected containing prohibited PII patterns.

Dashboards will distinguish an unavailable CLRS service from a disconnected kiosk. This is necessary to determine whether QR-1 is being met and whether graceful degradation is functioning.

## 5. Trade-off Ledger

| Risk | Likelihood / Impact | Measurable trigger | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concurrent reservations cause double booking | Medium / High | Any production incident or any failed concurrency test | Use database transaction isolation, exclusion or equivalent time-range constraints, and domain conflict checks. Run concurrent booking tests in CI. |
| Legacy inventory database is slow or unavailable | Medium / High | Import latency exceeds 60 seconds, or data is older than four hours | Use a read-only adapter and local synchronised cache. Alert on freshness. Continue serving from the last valid snapshot and document stale-data behaviour. |
| iCal feeds contain malformed or unexpected recurring events | Medium / Medium | More than 1% of feed entries fail parsing, or a feed import fails twice consecutively | Validate feeds, quarantine invalid entries, retain the previous valid snapshot and provide a staff-visible import status. |
| Kiosk updates exceed the ten-second requirement | Medium / High | More than 1% of reservation changes take over ten seconds to reach a connected kiosk | Use transactional outbox processing, indexed room lookups, update timestamps and retry queues. Load-test simultaneous kiosk updates. |
| SAML integration or role mapping is incorrect | Medium / High | More than 2% of test logins fail, or a staff account is granted student-only permissions incorrectly | Obtain representative test assertions early, implement explicit role mapping, add contract tests and require staff authorisation tests before release. |
| Search performance degrades at semester start | Medium / High | p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten minutes or database CPU exceeds 75% during load testing | Precompute local availability data, add indexes, use bounded caching, scale application instances and optimise slow queries before release. |
| Notification provider outage delays reminders | Medium / Medium | Provider error rate exceeds 5% or outbox age exceeds 15 minutes | Retry with exponential backoff, use idempotency keys, monitor the outbox and provide an operational replay mechanism. |
| A deployment or migration cannot be rolled back | Low / High | Rollback rehearsal takes more than ten minutes or migration is destructive | Use immutable images, backward-compatible migrations, automated rollback scripts and a mandatory rehearsal before production release. |
| Scope growth overwhelms the two-person team | High / Medium | More than two unplanned major features enter the release or a milestone slips by over one week | Freeze first-release scope, maintain a prioritised backlog and defer non-essential capabilities such as advanced analytics. |
| Sensitive data appears in logs or audit records | Low / High | Automated PII scan finds any email, SAML token or access token in application logs | Use structured logging with an allow-list, redact at the logging boundary, scan CI output and restrict audit-store access. |

The main architectural trade-off is accepting a modest amount of interface and adapter code in exchange for testability and integration isolation. If this discipline is not maintained, the modular monolith may accumulate design entropy and become a tightly coupled layered system. Code review rules and dependency checks will therefore prevent domain code from importing adapter or framework packages.

# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the existing study-room reservation tool used across three university libraries. Students and staff will search for rooms, create or change reservations, and cancel reservations. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Kiosks outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and the read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release includes room search, reservation management, staff block bookings, kiosk schedules, reminders and utilisation reports.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It does not specify implementation-level code or infrastructure configuration. The design prioritises reliable reservation rules, clear integration boundaries, straightforward operation by a two-person team and the ability to onboard additional libraries through configuration.

The principal quality targets are:

- 99.5% monthly availability during opening hours, with usable kiosk behaviour during network outages.
- Room-search p95 latency below 400 ms for 2,000 concurrent users.
- SAML authentication for all user actions, staff auditing and no personally identifiable information in logs.
- New campuses being added through configuration only.
- Reservation rules being testable without a database or network.
- Deployment and rollback being manageable by a two-person team, with rollback completed within 10 minutes.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **hexagonal architecture**, also known as ports-and-adapters architecture, as its primary architectural style.

The central domain/application core will contain reservation policies and use cases without depending on HTTP, SAML libraries, PostgreSQL, iCal, email, push-notification providers or kiosk protocols. External systems will communicate through explicit ports implemented by adapters.

The core will expose inbound ports such as:

- `SearchAvailability`
- `CreateReservation`
- `ModifyReservation`
- `CancelReservation`
- `CreateBlockBooking`
- `GetKioskSchedule`
- `ExportUtilisationReport`

It will depend on outbound ports such as:

- `RoomInventoryPort`
- `CalendarPort`
- `ReservationRepository`
- `NotificationPort`
- `KioskUpdatePort`
- `AuditPort`
- `ClockPort`

The HTTP API, SAML integration, PostgreSQL repository, iCal synchroniser, notification worker and kiosk delivery mechanism will be adapters around these ports.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
This is the strongest reason for selecting hexagonal architecture. Reservation rules are implemented in framework-independent domain services. Tests can provide in-memory reservations, a fake clock and fake room data without starting a database or contacting a network. Rules such as the three-hour daily limit, conflict detection, block-booking precedence and 48-hour notice can therefore be tested quickly and deterministically.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is kept at the inbound adapter boundary. The SAML adapter validates the identity-provider response and passes a trusted application identity and roles into the application core. Authorisation remains an explicit application concern rather than being scattered through controllers. Staff actions pass through an audit port. Log-writing adapters receive structured events that exclude names, email addresses and other PII.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Library-specific information—campus identifiers, opening hours, room mappings, equipment capabilities, calendar URLs and kiosk configuration—is held in configuration and validated at startup. The domain operates on campus and room abstractions rather than hard-coded library names. A fourth library can therefore be onboarded by adding validated configuration and data, without changing domain code.

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
The core has explicit adapters for external dependencies, allowing failures to be isolated. A temporary failure in iCal synchronisation must not prevent reservations using the last successful calendar snapshot. Kiosk adapters cache the latest valid schedule locally and display its timestamp when disconnected. The application can also be deployed as two identical instances behind a load balancer, while the database remains the source of truth for reservation writes.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
The architecture permits a dedicated availability query adapter and indexed read tables without exposing persistence details to the domain. Search can use precomputed room and calendar data, suitable indexes and short-lived caching. Reservation creation still performs an authoritative transactional conflict check. This separates the high-volume search path from the stricter write path.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
Hexagonal architecture does not require multiple independently deployed services. The initial release can be a small number of deployables: an API, a background worker and kiosk clients, sharing a versioned release. This reduces operational burden for a two-person team. Adapters can be replaced or upgraded independently in code while deployment remains simple. Versioned database migrations and immutable container images support rollback within 10 minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simpler to build and deploy and could meet the scale requirement. It was not selected as the primary style because traditional layers often allow application logic to become coupled to ORM models, web frameworks and database behaviour. That would make QR-5 weaker and make integration testing slower. It could also increase design entropy as new integrations and campus-specific exceptions accumulate.

Hexagonal architecture retains the operational simplicity of a monolith while making dependencies explicit. The cost is additional interfaces, dependency-injection configuration and adapter code. For a small first release, these costs are acceptable.

#### Microservices

Microservices would provide independent scaling and fault isolation. For example, search could scale separately from reporting and notification delivery. However, the expected system size and two-person operational team do not justify the cost of service discovery, distributed tracing, multiple deployment pipelines, network failure handling and cross-service data consistency.

Reservation creation, block-booking overrides and daily user limits are closely related transactional rules. Splitting them across services could create race conditions or require distributed transactions. Microservices are therefore rejected for the first release, although the ports provide a future extraction boundary if scale or team size changes.

#### Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log would be attractive for kiosk updates, audit history, reporting and high-volume search. It could make FR-4 naturally responsive by projecting reservation events into kiosk read models. However, it introduces eventual consistency, event replay, projection monitoring, schema evolution and operational recovery procedures. These are significant costs for a small initial system.

The selected design uses a transactional outbox and asynchronous update worker where useful, without making the whole system event-sourced or CQRS-based. The authoritative reservation transaction completes first; a reliable outbox event updates kiosks and notifications. This provides most of the required decoupling while keeping reservation decisions strongly consistent.

The diagram shows logical boundaries rather than necessarily separate processes. The API, core, adapters and persistence may be packaged in one application deployment. The worker may run as a second process using the same release artifact and database.

### 3.2 Main responsibilities

- **API adapter:** Validates request shape, maps HTTP responses and enforces rate limits.
- **SAML adapter:** Performs SAML login, validates assertions and maps users to application roles.
- **Domain core:** Applies reservation, opening-hours, conflict, notice and quota rules.
- **Availability query adapter:** Maintains searchable room and calendar information with indexes for campus, capacity, equipment and time.
- **Reservation repository adapter:** Performs transactional writes and authoritative overlap checks.
- **Inventory adapter:** Reads the legacy PostgreSQL database and converts records into the internal room model.
- **Calendar synchroniser:** Polls iCal feeds, validates entries and stores the last successful snapshot.
- **Transactional outbox:** Records outbound work in the same transaction as a reservation change.
- **Worker:** Processes outbox records, retries transient failures and updates notifications and kiosks.
- **Kiosk adapter:** Delivers updates and maintains the kiosk’s last-known schedule.
- **Audit adapter:** Stores staff-action audit records separately from ordinary operational logs.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search availability

1. The user authenticates through the SAML adapter and receives an application session or token.
2. The API adapter validates `campus`, capacity, equipment and time-window parameters.
3. The `SearchAvailability` inbound port passes a request object to the application core.
4. The core obtains configured opening hours and queries the availability query port.
5. The query adapter searches indexed room, equipment, calendar and reservation data.
6. Results are filtered for conflicts and returned with room details and availability intervals.
7. Room inventory and iCal data are refreshed asynchronously. If an external feed is temporarily unavailable, the last valid snapshot is used and its age is monitored.

The search path is read-optimised. Creating a reservation never relies only on search results: it repeats the conflict check in an authoritative database transaction to prevent two users reserving the same room simultaneously.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A reservation create, modify, cancel or block-booking transaction updates the reservation data and writes an outbox event atomically.
2. The worker reads the event and publishes a room-specific schedule update through the kiosk update port.
3. The kiosk receives the update through a push connection or polling endpoint and stores the schedule locally.
4. The kiosk displays the current and next reservation and records the update timestamp.
5. If the network or server is unavailable, the kiosk continues displaying its last-known schedule, clearly marked with its freshness time. On reconnection it polls for the latest complete schedule.
6. The service measures event-to-kiosk-update latency. The target is that at least 99% of updates arrive within 10 seconds.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit and domain tests

The largest test suite will target the framework-independent domain core. It will cover:

- Room overlap and conflict detection.
- Create, modify and cancel rules.
- The three-hour-per-day user limit.
- Opening-hours and campus configuration rules.
- Recurring block bookings.
- Staff permissions and 48-hour notice behaviour.
- Time-zone and daylight-saving transitions.
- Idempotency of repeated commands.
- Reminder scheduling at 15 minutes before start.

Fake repositories, a fake clock and in-memory room data will satisfy ports. These tests require no database or network and directly demonstrate QR-5. Boundary-value, property-based and mutation testing will be used for the most important reservation rules.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Integration tests will verify each adapter against realistic dependencies:

- PostgreSQL repository tests, including transaction isolation and overlap constraints.
- Migration tests from an empty database and from representative existing data.
- iCal parsing tests using valid, malformed, stale and timezone-changing feeds.
- SAML tests using signed test assertions, expired assertions, invalid audiences and role mappings.
- Notification-provider tests using a sandbox or stub.
- Kiosk connection, polling, reconnection and last-known-schedule behaviour.

Test containers or isolated CI databases will prevent tests from depending on developer machines.

#### Contract tests

Versioned contracts will be maintained for:

- HTTP request and response schemas.
- SAML attribute and role mapping expectations.
- iCal input assumptions.
- Notification-provider requests.
- Kiosk schedule responses and update messages.

Consumer-driven contract tests will ensure that API or kiosk changes do not silently break clients. Backward-compatible API changes will be preferred during rollout.

#### End-to-end tests

A small set of browser/API end-to-end tests will cover:

1. SAML login followed by room search.
2. Successful reservation creation.
3. Two concurrent reservation attempts for the same room, with exactly one success.
4. Modification and cancellation.
5. Staff block booking and the resulting student reservation behaviour.
6. Reservation change reaching a kiosk within the ten-second target.
7. Reminder creation and delivery through a test provider.
8. Monthly utilisation export.

End-to-end tests will run against a production-like environment but will not replace the faster unit and integration suites.

#### Performance, resilience and security testing

Before semester-start release:

- Load-test search with 2,000 concurrent users and representative campus data.
- Measure p50, p95 and p99 latency, error rate and database saturation.
- Run concurrent-write tests to identify conflicts and deadlocks.
- Inject failures into SAML, iCal, notification and kiosk connections.
- Verify that stale calendar data is handled safely.
- Run dependency, container and static-security scans.
- Test authorisation for student, staff and unauthenticated roles.
- Scan logs and traces to confirm that no PII is emitted.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development will use short-lived feature branches merged into `main` through pull requests. Each pull request requires code review by the other engineer where practical, passing automated checks and a linked requirement or defect.

CI gates are:

- Formatting, linting and static analysis.
- Unit/domain tests.
- Adapter integration tests.
- Contract tests.
- Security and dependency scanning.
- Database migration verification.
- Build of a versioned immutable container image.
- A smoke test in a temporary environment.

A release candidate must also pass end-to-end, load and resilience tests. Trunk-based development is preferred over long-lived branches to reduce merge divergence and design entropy.

Deployment will use a rolling or blue-green approach:

1. Build and sign an immutable image.
2. Apply backward-compatible database migrations.
3. Deploy the new API and worker beside the current version.
4. Run health checks and smoke tests.
5. Shift traffic gradually.
6. Monitor latency, error rate, reservation conflicts and outbox processing.

Database changes must be expand-and-contract: add new fields or tables first, deploy compatible application code, migrate data, then remove obsolete structures in a later release.

Rollback will be tested monthly and documented as a runbook. The previous image remains available, and traffic can be returned to it within 10 minutes. Migrations must be backward compatible so that application rollback does not require destructive database reversal. If a bad feature is isolated, configuration flags will disable it without a full redeployment.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Structured logs will include:

- Timestamp, severity, service version and correlation ID.
- Operation name and outcome.
- Campus and room identifiers where operationally necessary.
- Latency and dependency status.
- Reservation event type and idempotency result.
- Outbox retry count and kiosk update status.

Logs will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, session tokens, free-text user content or other PII. Reservation identifiers will be pseudonymous or hashed where possible. Staff audit records will contain the staff account identifier in a protected audit store, the action, target resource, timestamp and result; they are not ordinary application logs.

#### Metrics

Key metrics include:

- Opening-hours availability and successful-request rate.
- HTTP 5xx and dependency-failure rates.
- Search request count and p50/p95/p99 latency.
- Search timeout rate.
- Database CPU, connections, locks and slow queries.
- Reservation conflict rate and transaction failures.
- Age of the last successful iCal and inventory synchronisation.
- Outbox depth, oldest event age and retry count.
- Reservation-change-to-kiosk-update latency.
- Number and age of kiosks using stale schedules.
- Reminder queue delay and delivery success rate.

#### Alerts and service objectives

Alerts will include:

- Monthly availability projection below 99.5%, or an immediate sustained outage during opening hours.
- Search p95 above 400 ms for 10 consecutive minutes under normal traffic.
- Search error rate above 2% for five minutes.
- iCal or inventory snapshots older than the agreed freshness threshold.
- Outbox oldest event above 30 seconds or queue growth for five minutes.
- More than 1% of kiosk updates exceeding 10 seconds over a 15-minute window.
- Any kiosk remaining offline beyond the product-approved stale-schedule limit.
- Repeated SAML failures, unusual staff-action volume or audit-write failures.

Dashboards will show these measures by campus, allowing the team to distinguish a single-library failure from a system-wide failure.

# Campus Library Reservation System: Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, and cancel reservations. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Kiosks located outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities-calendar iCal feeds and the legacy read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release includes room search, reservation management, staff block bookings, kiosk schedules, reminders and utilisation reports.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It does not specify implementation-level details for every feature, nor does it attempt to replace detailed user stories or database design. The principal architectural goals are:

* keep reservation rules independent of infrastructure;
* isolate unreliable or externally controlled systems behind adapters;
* meet the 99.5% availability and 400 ms search-performance requirements;
* support configuration-only onboarding of future campuses;
* enable a two-person team to deploy and roll back safely.

The selected primary style is hexagonal architecture, implemented initially as a modular monolith. This provides a simple operational model while preserving boundaries that could support later extraction of selected components if scale or organisational needs justify it.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **hexagonal architecture**, also known as ports-and-adapters architecture, with a framework-independent domain core. The first deployment will be a modular monolith containing the application and domain modules in one deployable service.

The domain core will contain reservation entities, value objects and policies, including:

* time-window validation;
* the three-hour-per-day user limit;
* conflict detection;
* cancellation and modification rules;
* recurring block-booking rules;
* 48-hour notice validation;
* staff authorisation decisions;
* opening-hours constraints.

The domain core will not directly access HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email or push providers. Instead, it will use explicit inbound and outbound ports.

This decision supports the quality requirements as follows.

#### QR-1: Availability

A modular monolith reduces deployment and network failure points compared with a distributed microservice system. The service can be deployed redundantly behind a load balancer, with database backups and health checks.

The kiosk adapter stores the latest successfully retrieved schedule locally on the kiosk. If the service or network becomes unavailable, the kiosk displays the last-known schedule, its timestamp and an offline indicator. Reservation changes generate a schedule-update message through an application event and outbox mechanism. Kiosk clients receive updates through WebSocket or server-sent events, with polling as a fallback. This supports the ten-second refresh requirement without making kiosk availability dependent on a permanent connection.

#### QR-2: Performance

Search is implemented through an application port backed by a search-oriented persistence adapter. Room metadata from the legacy inventory database and availability data can be synchronised into locally indexed tables or an in-process/distributed cache. The search query can therefore avoid repeatedly querying the legacy database.

The system will be load-tested with 2,000 concurrent users. Database indexes will cover campus, capacity, equipment and reservation time ranges. Search results will be paginated and bounded. The architecture does not automatically guarantee performance, but it makes the performance-sensitive adapter replaceable without changing reservation rules.

#### QR-3: Security

Authentication is represented by an inbound identity port. A SAML adapter validates the university identity assertion and supplies a framework-independent authenticated-user object to the application layer. Staff authorisation is checked by application policies rather than by controllers alone.

Staff actions are sent to an audit port and persisted by an audit adapter. Application logs contain request IDs, operation names, campus and room identifiers, result codes and timing data, but not names, email addresses, SAML assertions or other PII. Sensitive values are redacted at the logging boundary.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

Campus, library, room, equipment, opening-hours and facilities-calendar settings are held in configuration and administrative data rather than hard-coded branches. A new campus can be onboarded by adding validated configuration, importing its inventory and assigning its calendar source. The application uses a common campus port and does not contain campus-specific business logic.

Configuration is version-controlled, schema-validated and promoted through the same delivery pipeline as application changes.

#### QR-5: Testability

The reservation use cases depend only on input values and injected ports such as `ReservationRepository`, `Clock`, `RoomAvailabilityPort`, `AuditPort` and `NotificationPort`. Unit tests can provide in-memory fakes and a fixed clock. They therefore test the three-hour limit, overlaps, recurring blocks and notice periods without a database or network.

This is the strongest reason for selecting hexagonal architecture: infrastructure concerns cannot become prerequisites for testing the rules.

#### QR-6: Operability

The modular monolith produces one primary application artifact, reducing the number of independently deployed components that the two-person team must operate. Container images are immutable and deployments are automated. A previous image can be restored within ten minutes using blue-green deployment or a rolling deployment with an immediately available previous version.

The trade-off is that a fault in one module may affect the whole application, so resource limits, timeouts, circuit breakers and database connection limits are required.

### 2.2 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A: Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simpler initially and could satisfy QR-6. It would also be efficient for a small team. However, ordinary layering often permits application code to depend directly on framework and persistence details. Over time, reservation rules could become coupled to ORM entities, HTTP controllers or database transactions. That would weaken QR-5 and increase design entropy.

The selected hexagonal structure retains the deployment simplicity of a monolith while enforcing stronger dependency direction. The cost is additional interfaces, adapters and up-front design work.

#### Method B: Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They could also isolate failures and allow teams to deploy components separately. However, the first release has a small operational team and a relatively bounded domain. Several services would introduce service discovery, API versioning, distributed tracing, multiple deployment pipelines and more failure modes. Reservation consistency and conflict detection would be more difficult if data were distributed.

Microservices would therefore make QR-6 harder to satisfy and could harm QR-1 through network and coordination failures. The selected modular monolith gives up independent scaling and independent deployment. If search or notifications later become dominant workloads, their hexagonal ports provide a possible extraction seam.

#### Method D: Event-driven architecture with CQRS

Event-driven CQRS would be attractive for kiosk updates, auditability, reporting and high-volume read models. It could make search and kiosk reads very fast and naturally support asynchronous notifications.

However, it introduces eventual consistency. A student could search a read model that is temporarily behind the authoritative reservation state. More importantly, event-log operation, replay, schema evolution, projection recovery and monitoring would add substantial complexity for the first release. Those costs conflict with QR-6.

The selected design uses a limited transactional outbox and application events for kiosk refreshes and notification work, but does not make the entire system event-sourced or CQRS-based. It gives up the full scalability and replayability of CQRS in exchange for simpler correctness and operations.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: room availability search

1. A client sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&equipment=&from=&to=`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates syntax, converts the request into a `SearchRoomsQuery` and obtains the authenticated user from the SAML adapter.
3. The application service checks access and invokes the `RoomSearchPort`.
4. The search adapter queries indexed room and reservation data. Inventory synchronisation imports room metadata from the legacy read-only PostgreSQL database; iCal imports provide facilities-calendar exclusions.
5. The application layer applies any final domain-level availability checks and maps results to a response DTO.
6. The HTTP adapter returns available rooms and relevant metadata.

Search data may be briefly stale during an import, but reservation creation always performs an authoritative conflict check in a transaction. This prevents a stale search result from creating a double booking.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden by a staff block booking.
2. The reservation use case commits the authoritative change and records a `RoomScheduleChanged` outbox entry in the same transaction.
3. A background publisher delivers the event to the kiosk-update adapter.
4. The adapter publishes the room-specific update through SSE/WebSocket. Kiosks also poll periodically to recover from missed messages.
5. The kiosk replaces its local schedule cache only after receiving a valid response and records the schedule version and retrieval time.
6. If the service or network is unavailable, the kiosk continues displaying the cached schedule and visibly reports its age.

The target is delivery to connected kiosks within ten seconds of the committed change. Retries and idempotent schedule versions prevent duplicate or out-of-order updates from corrupting displays.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover domain entities, policies and application services using fakes for every outbound port. They will test:

* overlapping reservations and conflict responses;
* the three-hour daily limit;
* modifications that would exceed the limit;
* recurring block bookings;
* 48-hour notice enforcement;
* opening-hours and time-zone boundaries;
* cancellation and authorisation rules;
* reminder scheduling;
* deterministic kiosk schedule generation.

A fake clock will test reminders and notice periods without waiting in real time. These tests directly satisfy QR-5. They should run on every commit and form the majority of the test suite.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Integration tests will verify adapters against disposable infrastructure:

* repository transactions and uniqueness/overlap constraints;
* search indexes and query plans;
* outbox publishing and retry behaviour;
* SAML assertion mapping using representative signed test assertions;
* iCal parsing, time zones and malformed feeds;
* legacy PostgreSQL connectivity and read-only enforcement;
* email/push provider integration;
* kiosk update delivery and reconnection.

These tests run in CI using containers or managed test services. External provider calls are not made against production.

#### Contract tests

Consumer-driven contracts will define the HTTP API, error formats and authentication expectations. Contracts will cover `409 Conflict`, validation errors, staff-only endpoints, pagination and kiosk schedule versions.

Provider verification will run before deployment. Adapter contracts will also ensure that a new campus configuration supplies all required fields and that imported inventory conforms to the expected schema.

#### End-to-end tests

A small, stable E2E suite will use a browser or API client against a deployed staging environment. It will verify:

* SAML login followed by room search;
* reservation creation and conflict handling;
* staff block booking and audit creation;
* kiosk update within the ten-second target;
* reminder creation;
* report export.

E2E tests will not attempt to cover every business-rule permutation; that responsibility belongs to unit tests. This keeps the suite useful and reduces false failures.

#### Performance, resilience and security tests

A load test will simulate at least 2,000 concurrent users at semester-start traffic levels, with search representing the expected majority of requests. The acceptance criterion is p95 search latency below 400 ms under the agreed workload, with error rate below one percent.

Resilience tests will stop the iCal importer, notification provider, kiosk connection and legacy inventory database independently. The service must time out rather than exhaust threads, continue using valid cached inventory where appropriate and preserve kiosk last-known schedules.

Security testing includes dependency scanning, static analysis, secret scanning, SAML signature and replay tests, authorisation tests, audit verification and a check that generated logs contain no PII.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development will use short-lived feature branches merged into `main` through pull requests. Every pull request requires review by the other engineer where practical, a successful CI pipeline and no unresolved high-severity security findings.

CI gates are:

1. formatting, linting and static analysis;
2. unit tests and coverage of domain/application modules;
3. adapter integration tests;
4. API and configuration contract tests;
5. dependency, container and secret scanning;
6. build of a versioned immutable container image.

Staging deployment runs integration, E2E and smoke tests. A performance test is required before the semester-start release and after changes to search or persistence.

Production deployment uses blue-green deployment:

1. build and sign the image once;
2. deploy the new version alongside the current version;
3. run health checks and smoke tests;
4. route a small percentage of traffic to the new version;
5. monitor error rate, latency, reservation conflicts and outbox lag;
6. switch all traffic only if acceptance thresholds remain satisfied.

Database changes use backward-compatible migrations. Destructive changes are separated from application releases so that the previous image remains runnable.

Rollback is performed by routing traffic back to the previous healthy image and disabling the new deployment. The previous image and migration status are retained. The rollback runbook is tested monthly and must complete within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6.

### 4.3 Observability

All requests receive a correlation ID. Structured logs record timestamp, correlation ID, endpoint, operation, campus identifier, room identifier where appropriate, status code, duration, retry count and failure category. User names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens and reservation descriptions are excluded or redacted. Staff audit records are stored separately from operational logs and contain the authorised staff identifier under the university’s approved retention policy.

Metrics include:

* successful request rate and error rate;
* monthly opening-hours availability;
* search latency p50, p95 and p99;
* search timeout and database connection-pool exhaustion;
* reservation conflict rate;
* outbox depth and oldest outbox age;
* kiosk update delivery latency;
* number and age of kiosks using stale schedules;
* iCal import freshness and failure count;
* notification queue delay and delivery failures;
* CPU, memory and database utilisation.

Alerts include:

* opening-hours availability forecast below 99.5%;
* search p95 above 350 ms for ten minutes, providing warning before the 400 ms limit;
* search p95 above 400 ms for five minutes;
* application error rate above two percent;
* outbox oldest item above two minutes or queue size above 1,000;
* kiosk updates exceeding ten seconds for more than one percent of changes;
* more than five percent of kiosks using schedules older than fifteen minutes;
* failed iCal or inventory imports for two consecutive runs.

Dashboards show these metrics by campus and library. Synthetic probes perform authenticated search and kiosk-schedule requests during opening hours. Logs, traces and metrics are retained according to university policy, with access restricted to the operations team.

# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the existing study-room reservation tool across three university libraries. Students and staff will search rooms, create and manage reservations, while library staff will administer rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Kiosks outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations. The system will integrate with the university SAML identity provider, facilities iCal feeds and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It covers the reservation, availability, block-booking, kiosk, notification and reporting capabilities, together with their external integrations. It does not define detailed user-interface designs, infrastructure procurement or the implementation of every individual API endpoint.

The principal goals are reliable reservation handling, fast availability searches, secure authentication and auditing, configuration-based onboarding of new campuses, testable reservation rules, and a deployment process manageable by a two-person team. The design prioritises a maintainable first release over maximum independent scalability of every subsystem.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)** as its primary architectural style. The initial deployment will be a modular monolith: one deployable application containing a framework-independent domain core and clearly separated adapters. Internal asynchronous processing will be used where appropriate, particularly for kiosk updates, reminders and reporting, but the system will not initially be built as a distributed event-driven platform.

The domain core owns reservation rules and does not depend on HTTP, databases, SAML, iCal or notification providers. External technologies communicate with the core through explicit inbound and outbound ports.

### 2.2 Rationale

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A modular monolith has fewer network and deployment failure points than a collection of microservices. The application can be deployed redundantly behind a load balancer, with a managed database and health checks. Kiosks retain the most recent valid schedule locally and display it with a timestamp when disconnected. Reservation changes publish an update through an outbox so that a temporary kiosk or notification failure does not invalidate the committed reservation.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability searches can use a dedicated indexed database query or cache adapter without requiring a network call between several services. Room, equipment and opening-hours data can be cached and indexed by campus, capacity and time range. The reservation command still performs an authoritative conflict check in the database. This separation allows search to meet the p95 target while preserving correctness for writes.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
A SAML adapter converts identity-provider assertions into an internal authenticated-user value. Domain use cases receive the user identity and role, rather than handling SAML details. Staff operations pass through an audit port. Structured logging is designed to record user and reservation identifiers only where necessary, with no names, email addresses or SAML assertions. Centralising authentication and authorisation in application adapters reduces the risk of inconsistent security checks.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific properties—library identifier, opening hours, rooms, equipment, time zone and facilities-calendar mapping—are stored as configuration and validated at startup. A new campus therefore uses the same domain logic and adapters without a code change. The inventory and calendar ports also isolate differences in external data formats.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation domain is framework-independent and communicates through interfaces such as `ReservationRepository`, `Clock`, `AvailabilityReader` and `AuditWriter`. Unit tests can provide in-memory fakes for these ports. Rules such as the three-hour daily limit, overlap prevention, staff override and 48-hour notice can therefore be tested without a database or network.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A modular monolith is appropriate for a two-person team. There is one application artifact, one release pipeline and one primary rollback operation. Database changes will use backward-compatible migrations, allowing the previous application version to continue running during rollback. Immutable container images and a blue/green or rolling deployment support rollback within ten minutes.

The architecture also supports FR-4 and FR-5 through an outbox and worker mechanism. A successful reservation transaction writes both the reservation and an outbound event record. A worker publishes the event to kiosk-update and reminder adapters. This avoids coupling the user-facing request to the availability of email, push or kiosk connections.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

**Layered monolith.**  
A layered monolith would be simple to deploy and could meet the operational target. However, conventional layered designs often allow application and domain code to become coupled to ORM models, HTTP controllers or vendor-specific infrastructure. That would weaken QR-5 and make external integration changes more expensive. Hexagonal architecture adds interfaces and mapping code, but provides stronger dependency boundaries and more reliable unit testing. The chosen design gives up some initial implementation simplicity in exchange for lower long-term design entropy.

**Microservices.**  
Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting and isolate some failures. However, they introduce service discovery, network retries, distributed tracing, multiple deployment pipelines and cross-service data consistency. These costs are disproportionate for three libraries and a two-person operational team. Microservices would make QR-6 more difficult and could make reservation conflict handling harder. The chosen modular boundaries preserve the option to extract a component later if monitoring shows a genuine scaling or ownership need. The trade-off is that the first deployment cannot independently scale each module.

**Event-driven architecture with CQRS.**  
CQRS would provide excellent scalability for search and kiosks and naturally support asynchronous projections. It could also improve resilience for read-heavy workloads. However, event-log retention, replay, projection correctness, eventual consistency and operational recovery add substantial complexity. A stale availability projection could be problematic when users are making reservations, even if the authoritative command model is correct. The selected design uses an outbox and selective read caching, gaining much of the required asynchronous behaviour without making all data eventually consistent. The trade-off is less independent read scaling and less natural historical event replay.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. The user authenticates through the SAML adapter and receives a CLRS session or token containing an internal user identifier and role.
2. The REST adapter validates the request parameters: campus, capacity, equipment, start time and end time.
3. The application service invokes the `SearchAvailability` use case.
4. The use case obtains room metadata from the inventory port and opening hours from the configuration/calendar ports.
5. The availability adapter executes an indexed query against reservations and block bookings. A short-lived cache may be used for room metadata and stable calendar information.
6. The domain policy excludes rooms with conflicting reservations, facilities closures or insufficient capacity/equipment.
7. The response is mapped to a public API representation. Logs contain latency, campus code and result count, but not personal information.

For creating or modifying a reservation, the search result is not treated as authoritative. The command use case performs a final transactional conflict check using a database constraint or serialisable transaction. A conflict returns HTTP 409.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A reservation, cancellation or block-booking command is validated by the domain and committed transactionally.
2. The same transaction writes a room-specific outbox message containing the room identifier, event type and new schedule version.
3. A worker reads the outbox and updates the kiosk schedule cache, then notifies connected kiosks or makes the new version available to polling kiosks.
4. Each kiosk polls or receives a push notification and requests the latest schedule using its room identifier.
5. The kiosk stores the last successful schedule locally. If the network is unavailable, it continues to display that schedule with its last-updated time and an offline indicator.
6. Metrics measure the time from reservation commit to kiosk acknowledgement. The target is that at least 99% of changes reach the relevant kiosk within ten seconds.

A failed notification is retried with exponential backoff. Messages are idempotent using the schedule version, so retries cannot corrupt the display.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

**Domain unit tests.**  
These are the largest test group and run without a database or network. They cover:

- no overlapping reservations;
- the three-hour-per-day user limit;
- reservation creation, modification and cancellation;
- recurring block bookings;
- 48-hour notice rules and staff override behaviour;
- opening-hours and closure rules;
- campus configuration validation;
- time-zone and daylight-saving boundary cases;
- authorisation decisions for student and staff actions.

A fake clock makes reminder and notice-period tests deterministic. Fake repositories and audit ports satisfy QR-5.

**Application-service tests.**  
These verify orchestration and port interactions using mocks or in-memory adapters. They check that staff actions create audit records, failed commands do not publish events, successful commands create outbox messages, and duplicate requests are handled idempotently.

**Adapter and integration tests.**  
Database integration tests run against a disposable PostgreSQL instance and cover transaction isolation, unique/conflict constraints, migrations, indexes and report queries. SAML adapter tests use representative signed assertions and invalid/expired assertions. iCal tests cover malformed feeds, time zones and feed outages. Legacy inventory tests verify read-only access and schema mapping.

**Contract tests.**  
The REST API has an OpenAPI contract tested against the consumer UI and kiosk client. Adapter contract tests verify the expected SAML, iCal, notification-provider and inventory interfaces. These tests detect incompatible changes before deployment.

**End-to-end tests.**  
A small suite runs in a staging environment with SAML test identities. It covers login, search, create/modify/cancel, staff block booking, conflict responses, kiosk update propagation and reminder scheduling. It also tests the offline kiosk fallback by disabling network access.

**Performance and resilience tests.**  
A load test simulates 2,000 concurrent users at semester-start traffic levels, measuring search p95, error rate and database saturation. Failure tests stop the iCal feed, notification provider and kiosk connection to verify graceful degradation. A deployment rehearsal demonstrates rollback within ten minutes.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development uses short-lived branches and pull requests into `main`. Every pull request must pass formatting, static analysis, dependency/security scanning, unit tests, integration tests and API contract tests. A merge requires review by the second team member. Main builds an immutable versioned container.

The pipeline deploys automatically to a test environment, then to staging after end-to-end and performance smoke tests. Production deployment uses a backward-compatible database migration followed by a canary instance. Health checks include database connectivity, outbox-worker health and representative search latency. Traffic is gradually moved to the new version while error rate and p95 latency are monitored.

Rollback consists of directing traffic to the previous image and, if necessary, disabling the new feature through configuration. Schema changes follow expand-and-contract migration rules: add compatible fields first, deploy code, migrate data, and remove obsolete fields only in a later release. The rollback procedure is rehearsed at least once per semester and must complete within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6.

### 4.3 Observability

**Logs**

Structured logs include timestamp, severity, correlation ID, endpoint, outcome, duration, campus code, room code where operationally necessary, reservation ID and error category. Staff actions produce a separate tamper-resistant audit record containing authenticated staff identifier, action, target entity, timestamp and result. Logs do not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, session tokens, notification contents or other PII. Identifiers are access-controlled and retained only for the approved period.

**Metrics**

- HTTP request count, error rate and latency by endpoint;
- availability-search p50, p95 and p99 latency;
- concurrent users and database connection utilisation;
- reservation conflict rate;
- outbox backlog size and oldest message age;
- reservation-commit-to-kiosk-update latency;
- percentage of kiosk updates completed within ten seconds;
- kiosk heartbeat and offline duration;
- SAML authentication failures and external dependency failures;
- notification delivery and retry rates;
- uptime during configured opening hours.

**Tracing**

Distributed correlation IDs connect an HTTP request, database transaction, outbox message and kiosk update. Traces record timing and dependency names but exclude request bodies containing personal data.

**Alerts**

- opening-hours synthetic checks fail for five consecutive minutes;
- rolling monthly availability falls below the QR-1 budget or a five-minute error-rate threshold is exceeded;
- availability-search p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under normal traffic;
- database CPU exceeds 80% for ten minutes or connection pool exhaustion occurs;
- outbox oldest-message age exceeds two minutes;
- more than 1% of kiosk changes miss the ten-second target over fifteen minutes;
- SAML or inventory failures exceed an agreed rate.

Dashboards show the monthly QR-1 calculation, current dependency health, search latency and kiosk freshness by campus.

# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and Scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students, staff, library kiosks and administrative reporting across three campus libraries.

Students and staff will authenticate through the university’s SAML identity provider. Students will search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, and cancel them. Staff will manage rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Block bookings may override student reservations when at least 48 hours’ notice is provided. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservation, while users will receive reminders before reservations begin. The system will integrate with facilities iCal feeds and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.

This document covers the first-release architecture, quality plan, delivery approach, operational monitoring and major risks. It does not specify implementation-level code or the complete user interface.

The principal quality goals are:

- 99.5% availability during opening hours, with useful kiosk behaviour during connectivity loss.
- Availability-search p95 latency below 400 ms under 2,000 concurrent users.
- SAML authentication, staff auditing and protection of personally identifiable information in logs.
- Configuration-only onboarding of a new campus.
- Database- and network-independent testing of reservation rules.
- Deployment and rollback by a two-person team, with rollback completed within 10 minutes.

---

## 2. Architectural Decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **hexagonal architecture** as its primary architectural style. The reservation domain will be a framework-independent core surrounded by application use cases, inbound ports and outbound ports. External technologies such as HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email, push notifications and kiosk communication will be implemented as replaceable adapters.

The system will initially be delivered as one deployable application, with a separate kiosk client. Hexagonal architecture is compatible with this deployment choice: it defines dependency direction and boundaries without requiring microservices. Where useful, asynchronous processing will be used inside the application for notifications, reports and kiosk updates, but CLRS will not adopt event-driven CQRS as its primary style.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
This is the strongest reason for the decision. Reservation rules will be implemented in the domain core and called through use-case services. The core will depend only on abstractions such as `ReservationRepository`, `RoomAvailabilityPort` and `Clock`. Unit tests can provide in-memory or fake implementations of these ports, so rules can be tested without a database or network. Examples include:

- the three-hour daily user limit;
- overlapping reservation prevention;
- block-booking precedence;
- the 48-hour notice rule;
- modification and cancellation permissions;
- recurring booking expansion.

This avoids coupling business rules to HTTP frameworks, SQL queries or SAML libraries.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific information will be configuration rather than code. A campus configuration will define its campus identifier, opening hours, rooms, equipment, time zone, facilities-calendar feed and inventory mapping. The inventory and calendar adapters translate external representations into domain objects. Adding a fourth campus should therefore require configuration, data validation and deployment, but no change to domain logic.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is isolated behind an inbound SAML adapter. The application receives a normalised authenticated identity and roles rather than depending on SAML details throughout the domain. Staff-only use cases enforce authorisation and emit audit records through an `AuditPort`. Logging is also behind an operational logging boundary, allowing identifiers to be redacted or pseudonymised consistently. This supports authenticated actions, staff auditing and a policy forbidding names, email addresses and SAML assertions in ordinary logs.

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
The core reservation service can remain available if an external read-only dependency is temporarily unavailable. Inventory and iCal data will be synchronised into a local read cache. Search can use the most recent valid cache, with its freshness shown in operational metrics. Kiosk adapters persist the last-known schedule locally and display it with a “last updated” timestamp when disconnected. The architecture therefore prevents every kiosk display from depending on a live central request.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
The availability-search use case can use a local indexed read model or cache populated by the inventory and calendar adapters. Search does not need to query the legacy PostgreSQL database or iCal feeds synchronously. Reservation creation still performs an authoritative conflict check through the reservation repository. Separating the search representation from external systems reduces latency and protects those systems from the semester-start traffic spike.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A single main deployment is more practical for a two-person team than several independently deployed services. Health checks, database migrations, configuration validation and containerised deployment can be standardised. Immutable versioned images and a previous-version rollback support the ten-minute rollback requirement.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

**Layered monolith.**  
A layered monolith would be simple to understand and deploy. It could meet the initial operational requirement, but layers alone do not guarantee that the domain is independent of frameworks or infrastructure. Business rules may gradually leak into controllers, ORM models and SQL, making QR-5 harder to maintain. A layered design also provides weaker explicit boundaries around external integrations. Hexagonal architecture retains the monolith’s deployment simplicity while enforcing stronger dependency boundaries. The trade-off is additional interfaces and adapter code.

**Microservices.**  
Separate reservation, inventory, notification and reporting services could provide independent scaling and fault isolation. For example, reporting could be scaled without affecting reservation traffic. However, this would introduce network calls, distributed tracing, service discovery, multiple deployment pipelines and cross-service data consistency. It would be disproportionate for a two-person operations team and would make ten-minute rollback more difficult. Microservices could also make reservation conflict handling and transactional consistency harder. CLRS gives up independent service scaling in favour of simpler deployment and stronger transactional control.

**Event-driven architecture with CQRS.**  
CQRS projections would be attractive for high-volume search and kiosk updates. Events could also provide a strong audit history and naturally trigger reminders. However, event ordering, replay, duplicate delivery, projection lag and schema evolution introduce substantial complexity. The system would need clear recovery procedures if a kiosk projection became stale. CLRS instead uses a transactional reservation model with an outbox for reliable asynchronous notifications and kiosk invalidations. This gives up some scalability and real-time projection flexibility, but keeps the first release easier to reason about. If load or integration requirements grow, the outbox can later feed dedicated projections without changing the domain ports.

The main architectural cost is a risk of interface proliferation and duplicated mapping code. This will be controlled through shared adapter conventions, architecture tests and regular removal of unused ports. Otherwise, accumulated design entropy could make the architecture appear hexagonal while allowing infrastructure dependencies to leak into the core.

### 3.2 Main components

- **Inbound HTTP adapter:** validates requests, maps them to commands and returns HTTP responses such as `409 Conflict` for reservation conflicts.
- **SAML adapter:** validates SAML assertions and maps users to internal identifiers and roles.
- **Application use cases:** coordinates commands such as create reservation, modify reservation, cancel reservation, create block booking and export report.
- **Reservation domain:** owns entities, value objects, policies and invariants.
- **Reservation repository adapter:** performs authoritative persistence and conflict-safe writes.
- **Search port and cache:** provides fast availability queries using normalised room, opening-hour, calendar and reservation data.
- **Inventory and iCal adapters:** periodically import external data and record freshness and import failures.
- **Outbox:** stores notification and kiosk-update messages in the same transaction as reservation changes.
- **Notification adapter:** sends email and push reminders.
- **Kiosk adapter:** publishes room schedule changes and supports kiosk polling. The kiosk stores the last successful schedule locally.
- **Audit adapter:** records staff actions with actor identifier, action, target, timestamp and result, without writing unnecessary PII.
- **Reporting adapter:** calculates or exports monthly campus utilisation from reservation and opening-hour data.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. The client sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&equipment=&from=&to=` to the HTTP adapter.
2. The SAML adapter confirms the session and supplies the internal user identity.
3. The adapter validates the time window and maps the request to the `SearchAvailability` use case.
4. The use case calls the availability-search port. It reads a locally indexed cache containing room attributes, opening hours, facilities-calendar exclusions and reservation summaries.
5. The search component filters by campus, capacity and equipment, then removes rooms with conflicts during the requested window.
6. The response includes matching rooms and, where relevant, the freshness time of external data.
7. If the inventory or iCal import is unavailable, the latest validated cache remains usable. An alert is raised if its age exceeds the agreed threshold.

Search is read-optimised and does not synchronously query the legacy database or external calendar, supporting QR-2.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A reservation, modification, cancellation or staff block booking is accepted by the reservation use case.
2. The transaction writes the reservation change and a room-specific kiosk-update message to the database outbox.
3. A background worker delivers the update through the kiosk update adapter. The adapter may use push or kiosk polling.
4. Each kiosk validates the message, stores the new schedule locally and displays it.
5. If communication fails, the kiosk continues displaying its last-known schedule and shows its timestamp. It does not accept reservations locally.
6. The service records the reservation-change time and kiosk-acknowledgement time. The target is acknowledgement and display update within 10 seconds.

Retries are idempotent using a change identifier, preventing duplicate updates.

## 4. Quality Plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

**Domain unit tests.**  
These are the largest test category. They instantiate domain objects and use fake clocks, repositories and identity policies. They cover all reservation rules, including overlap boundaries, daily limits, recurring bookings, block-booking precedence, notice periods, authorisation decisions and cancellation/modification rules. They require no database or network, directly satisfying QR-5.

Property-based tests will generate time intervals and reservation combinations to test invariants such as “two accepted reservations for the same room cannot overlap” and “a user’s accepted student reservations do not exceed three hours per day.”

**Application-service tests.**  
These test use-case orchestration using fake ports. They verify transaction behaviour, outbox creation, audit invocation, error mapping and idempotency. For example, a successful reservation must create exactly one kiosk update and one reminder request; a rejected reservation must create neither.

**Adapter unit tests.**  
HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, notification and kiosk adapters will be tested with representative fixtures. Sensitive SAML cases include expired assertions, invalid signatures, replay attempts and incorrect role mappings. Logging tests will verify that test requests containing names or email addresses do not emit those values.

**Integration tests.**  
Containerised tests will run against a real supported database and message/outbox worker. They will verify transaction boundaries, unique conflict constraints, migrations, indexes, cache refreshes and retry behaviour. External providers will be replaced by deterministic test servers.

**Contract tests.**  
Provider contracts will cover the CLRS HTTP API, kiosk schedule format, SAML claim mapping, facilities iCal interpretation and notification-provider requests. Consumer tests will ensure that a kiosk can process schedule versions and that API changes do not break clients. Contracts will be versioned and run in CI.

**End-to-end tests.**  
A small suite will exercise SAML login, search, reservation creation, conflict response, cancellation, staff block booking, kiosk update and reminder scheduling in a staging environment. These tests will cover critical journeys rather than every business-rule combination.

**Performance and resilience tests.**  
A load test will simulate 2,000 concurrent users performing realistic searches, with a smaller proportion creating reservations. The acceptance target is p95 search latency below 400 ms and no unacceptable increase in conflict errors. Failure tests will disable iCal, inventory, notification and kiosk connections to verify cached search, retries and graceful kiosk degradation.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development will use short-lived feature branches and pull requests into `main`. Every pull request must pass:

- compilation, formatting and static analysis;
- domain unit tests and coverage of all reservation policies;
- adapter, integration and contract tests;
- dependency and container vulnerability scanning;
- architecture tests confirming that the domain has no infrastructure dependencies;
- database migration checks;
- a smoke performance test.

Merges to `main` produce an immutable, versioned container image. Deployment will use a staging environment followed by a canary release during a monitored period. Database changes must be backwards-compatible: expand the schema, deploy code, migrate data, then remove obsolete fields only after rollback is no longer required.

Production deployment will use health checks, automated configuration validation and a documented runbook usable by two people. The previous image and configuration remain available. If health checks fail, error rate rises, or latency breaches the release threshold, traffic is switched back to the previous version. Rollback is rehearsed monthly and must complete within 10 minutes. Outbox messages are retained during rollback so that notifications and kiosk changes are not silently lost.

### 4.3 Observability

For **QR-1**, the system will measure:

- successful and failed HTTP requests by endpoint;
- availability during configured opening hours;
- database connection and transaction failures;
- SAML authentication failures and latency;
- inventory and iCal import success, failure and data age;
- outbox backlog and worker failure rate;
- kiosk connection status, last successful update and update age;
- reservation-change-to-kiosk-acknowledgement time.

Alerts will include:

- projected monthly availability below 99.5%;
- five-minute error rate above 2%;
- no successful inventory or iCal refresh for 15 minutes, or an agreed longer threshold based on feed frequency;
- any kiosk without a successful update for 60 seconds during active operation;
- kiosk update p95 above 10 seconds;
- growing outbox backlog for five minutes.

For **QR-2**, the service will publish p50, p95 and p99 latency for availability search, tagged by campus and response status. It will also measure request rate, cache hit rate, database query latency, CPU, memory, connection-pool saturation and timeouts. Alerts will fire when search p95 exceeds 400 ms for five consecutive minutes under normal traffic, or when load-test projections show the threshold will fail at 2,000 concurrent users.

Logs will use correlation IDs, endpoint, status, duration, campus identifier and internal non-PII resource identifiers. They will never contain SAML assertions, access tokens, names, email addresses or free-text user data. Staff audit records are stored separately with controlled access. Metrics and traces will be sampled and retained according to university policy.
